items.setupText: The morning shift handles 40 parcels; the evening shift handles 80.
items.taskText: Choose the grammatically correct completion: The evening shift handles twice ___ the morning shift.
options: as much parcels as
many parcels than
as many parcels as
as many parcels than
items.answer: as many parcels as
items.explanation: 'Twice as many parcels as' compares two counts and expresses a two-to-one ratio.

rationales.as much parcels as: Parcels are separate countable items, so use 'many' rather than 'much'.
rationales.as many parcels as: 'Twice as many parcels as' compares two counts and expresses a two-to-one ratio.
rationales.many parcels than: The twice construction here needs as many ... as, not many ... than.
rationales.as many parcels than: The second comparison word must be 'as' in 'twice as many ... as'.

findings: The busier-front-desk item had an incoherent handbook tail and elementary repeated foils.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts count-based ratios with amount-based ones.
audit.levelReason: Simple workplace totals keep attention on the multiword structure.

items.setupText: A supplier offers two screens. 'This one is bigger, but the other is brighter.'
items.taskText: Which summary preserves both comparisons?

The bigger screen is also the brighter one.
The screens are equal in size but differ in brightness.
The screens differ in size but have equal brightness.
items.answer: Neither screen leads on both size and brightness.
items.explanation: One screen leads on size, while the other leads on brightness; the advantages are split.

rationales.The bigger screen is also the brighter o: The supplier assigns greater brightness to the other screen.
rationales.The screens are equal in size but differ: Bigger states a size difference, so equality loses part of the comparison.
rationales.Neither screen leads on both size and br: One screen leads on size, while the other leads on brightness; the advantages are split.
rationales.The screens differ in size but have equa: The other is brighter explicitly states a brightness difference as well as a size difference.

findings: The newer-badge comparison added only a contextual tail to the same form choice.
audit.microSkill: Tracking two comparisons with different winners
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps separate dimensions from collapsing into one overall ranking.
audit.levelReason: Concrete product properties support a two-part comparison.
audit.similarityNote: A trade-off between dimensions, unlike a single relative-risk inference.

items.setupText: A visitor says, 'This is the most interesting tour I've ever taken.'
items.taskText: Which group is the visitor using for the comparison?
options: All tours currently available in the city
All the tours the visitor has taken up to now
Only tours taken during the current holiday
All tours that other visitors have recommended
items.answer: All the tours the visitor has taken up to now
items.explanation: I've ever taken defines a personal experience set extending up to the present.

rationales.All tours currently available in the cit: The relative clause limits the group to tours the visitor has taken, not all available tours.
rationales.Only tours taken during the current holi: Ever includes earlier experience too, unless the context separately restricts it.
rationales.All tours that other visitors have recom: Recommendations are not the same as the speaker's own experience.
rationales.All the tours the visitor has taken up t: I've ever taken defines a personal experience set extending up to the present.

findings: The older guide was older repeated its answer in the subject and offered no new skill.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies the comparison set rather than reading a personal judgment as universal.
audit.levelReason: A common travel reaction combines a superlative with familiar present-perfect experience.
audit.similarityNote: Experience-bounded ranking, not an unrestricted group superlative.

items.setupText: Three meeting rooms hold 20, 35, and 50 people respectively.
items.taskText: Which capacity belongs to the second-largest room by seating capacity?
options: 50 people
20 people
35 people
Either 35 or 50 people
items.answer: 35 people
items.explanation: 'Second-largest' means one place below the largest; 35 lies between 50 and 20.

rationales.35 people: 'Second-largest' means one place below the largest; 35 lies between 50 and 20.
rationales.50 people: Fifty is the largest capacity, not the second-largest.
rationales.20 people: Twenty is the smallest capacity, two places below the largest in this group.
rationales.Either 35 or 50 people: 'Second-largest' names a single rank here; the different capacities leave no tie.

findings: The stronger-voice item repeated much plus a basic comparative under a training tail.
audit.microSkill: An ordinal modifying a superlative rank
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets second-largest as a precise position in an ordered set.

audit.similarityNote: An intermediate rank rather than selecting the maximum or minimum.

items.setupText: The metal stand costs more but lasts longer than the plastic stand.
items.taskText: Which sentence preserves both relations while starting with the plastic stand?
options: The plastic stand is cheaper and more durable.
The plastic stand is dearer but less durable.
The plastic stand is cheaper but less durable.
The plastic stand is dearer and more durable.
items.answer: The plastic stand is cheaper but less durable.
items.explanation: Reversing the products makes the plastic one lower in both cost and durability.

rationales.The plastic stand is cheaper and more du: Cheaper preserves the price relation, but more durable reverses the lifetime relation.
rationales.The plastic stand is cheaper but less du: Reversing the products makes the plastic one lower in both cost and durability.
rationales.The plastic stand is dearer but less dur: Less durable is right, but dearer incorrectly gives plastic the higher price.
rationales.The plastic stand is dearer and more dur: Both comparisons are reversed: plastic costs less and lasts less long.

findings: The claim becoming weaker after an example was added had no useful rationale and repeated mechanical foils.
audit.microSkill: Reversing a two-dimensional comparative description
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves a practical trade-off when changing the subject of the comparison.
audit.levelReason: Familiar cost and lifetime properties support a compact two-step paraphrase.
audit.similarityNote: Rewrites both relations; 775 only interprets split product advantages.

items.setupText: As the course progresses, each task requires more effort than the previous one.
items.taskText: Choose the standard completion that describes this trend: 'The tasks are becoming ___'.
options: most and most demanding
more demanding and more
more and more demanding
more and demanding
items.answer: more and more demanding
items.explanation: Repeating 'more' around 'and' expresses a growing degree with a longer adjective.

rationales.most and most demanding: 'Most' is a superlative; repeating it does not form this increasing-degree expression.
rationales.more demanding and more: The repeated degree words belong together before demanding: more and more demanding.
rationales.more and more demanding: Repeating 'more' around 'and' expresses a growing degree with a longer adjective.
rationales.more and demanding: The second comparative marker is missing; and cannot join more directly to demanding this way.

findings: The closer-entrance item repeated the same frame and irrelevant checklist context.
audit.microSkill: More and more with a longer adjective
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends progressive comparison beyond short forms such as colder and colder.
audit.levelReason: A familiar course progression supports a longer comparative structure.
audit.similarityNote: Long-adjective trend formation, not A2's quantity trend or short-adjective interpretation.

items.setupText: Two notices say 'The new stop is farther from the school' and 'The new stop is further from the school.'
items.taskText: Which comment on these distance comparisons is accurate in standard English?
options: Both farther and further can compare physical distance.
Only 'farther' can refer to physical distance.
Only 'further' can refer to physical distance.
'Farther' and 'further' describe equal distances.
items.answer: Both farther and further can compare physical distance.
items.explanation: For physical distance, farther and further are both established alternatives; this context does not force one.

rationales.Only 'farther' can refer to physical dis: Further also commonly compares physical distance; it is not restricted to figurative uses.
rationales.Only 'further' can refer to physical dis: 'Farther' is a standard physical-distance comparative too.
rationales.'Farther' and 'further' describe equal d: Both are comparative forms of far; neither expresses equality here.
rationales.Both farther and further can compare phy: For physical distance, farther and further are both established alternatives; this context does not force one.

findings: The original farther item missed a useful legitimate-variant distinction and repeated elementary malformed foils.
audit.microSkill: Farther and further as valid distance alternatives
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents an artificial rule from excluding a standard variant.
audit.levelReason: A short transport comparison supports recognition of common alternatives.
audit.similarityNote: Explicitly accepts alternative comparative forms rather than manufacturing a unique spelling answer.

items.setupText: A: 'The appendices can wait; only the main report matters.' B: 'The appendices are no less useful than the main report.'
items.taskText: Which reading of B's comparison is supported?
options: B ranks the appendices as slightly less useful than the report.
B says the appendices are useful only when read after the report.
B rejects placing the appendices below the report in usefulness.
B ranks the appendices above the report by a small amount.
items.answer: B rejects placing the appendices below the report in usefulness.
items.explanation: No less useful denies inferiority on that scale; it counters A's dismissal without requiring that the appendices be superior.

rationales.B rejects placing the appendices below t: No less useful denies inferiority on that scale; it counters A's dismissal without requiring that the appendices be superior.
rationales.B ranks the appendices as slightly less: No negates the lower ranking; it does not merely reduce the size of a disadvantage.
rationales.B says the appendices are useful only wh: The comparison addresses usefulness, not a required reading order.
rationales.B ranks the appendices above the report: They may be equally useful; no less does not require a positive lead.

findings: The most-useful report cloze was elementary, repeated four times, and explained as comparative rather than superlative.
audit.microSkill: No less plus adjective denying inferiority
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates equality-compatible rejection of inferiority from asserted superiority.
audit.levelReason: A natural rebuttal requires interpreting comparative negation and stance.
audit.similarityNote: No less in a rebuttal, distinct from numeric minimum instructions.

items.setupText: After viewing two charts, a reader says, 'The first isn't nearly as clear as the revised one.'
items.taskText: Which paraphrase best preserves the strength and direction of the comparison?
options: The revised chart is only slightly clearer than the first.
The revised chart is considerably less clear than the first.
The revised chart is considerably clearer than the first.
The revised chart is almost as clear as the first.
items.answer: The revised chart is considerably clearer than the first.
items.explanation: Not nearly as ... as places the first well below the revised chart in clarity.

rationales.The revised chart is only slightly clear: Not nearly as clear marks a substantial gap, not just a slight improvement.
rationales.The revised chart is considerably cleare: Not nearly as ... as places the first well below the revised chart in clarity.
rationales.The revised chart is considerably less c: This reverses which chart is clearer.
rationales.The revised chart is almost as clear as: Almost as clear places the revised chart slightly below the first, changing both direction and degree.

findings: The far-more-clear cloze used elementary scrambled foils and was repeated with only context tails.
audit.microSkill: Not nearly as ... as marking a substantial gap
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves both degree and direction when paraphrasing negative equality.
audit.levelReason: A multiword degree phrase requires more than basic comparative recognition.
audit.similarityNote: A large negative-equality gap, not the earlier small-improvement dialogue.

items.setupText: In an informal conversation about three rooms, one guest says 'This room is cheapest of the three'; another says 'This room is the cheapest of the three.'
items.taskText: Which editorial comment is accurate?
options: Only the version with the can express a group ranking.
The bare version compares two rooms; the version with the compares three.
The bare version means 'very cheap' without comparing the rooms.
Both can express the same lowest-price ranking in this context.
items.answer: Both can express the same lowest-price ranking in this context.
items.explanation: After 'is' with no following noun, informal English permits 'the' to be omitted here; both versions rank this room lowest in price.

rationales.Only the version with the can express a: A predicative superlative without a following noun can omit 'the' in informal use and still rank the group.
rationales.The bare version compares two rooms; the: The phrase 'of the three' sets the group in both versions; article choice does not change its size.
rationales.Both can express the same lowest-price r: After 'is' with no following noun, informal English permits 'the' to be omitted here; both versions rank this room lowest in price.
rationales.The bare version means 'very cheap' with: Cheapest and of the three still supply a superlative ranking; omitting the does not turn it into very cheap.

findings: The original schedule superlative used faulty boilerplate and underconstrained comparative alternatives.
audit.microSkill: Optional the with an informal predicative superlative
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents rejection of an established bare-superlative construction.
audit.levelReason: Comparing two valid edits requires sensitivity to syntax and register.
audit.similarityNote: Directly addresses article optionality, without the Articles topic's a most attributive intensifier frame.

items.setupText: The organiser writes, 'The instructions are all the easier to follow for having a diagram.'
items.taskText: What role does the diagram have in this comparison?
options: It contributes to making the instructions easier to follow.
It makes every instruction equally easy to follow.
It compensates for instructions that have become harder overall.
It is compared with the instructions as an alternative set of directions.
items.answer: It contributes to making the instructions easier to follow.
items.explanation: All the plus a comparative, followed by a reason, presents that reason as adding to the degree described.

rationales.It makes every instruction equally easy: All the easier strengthens an improvement; all does not distribute equal ease across every instruction.
rationales.It compensates for instructions that hav: The phrase attributes increased ease to the diagram; it does not report an overall deterioration.
rationales.It is compared with the instructions as: For having a diagram gives a reason for the increased ease, not a second set of instructions being ranked.
rationales.It contributes to making the instruction: All the plus a comparative, followed by a reason, presents that reason as adding to the degree described.

findings: The slightly cloze tested basic adjective/adverb forms and appeared four times with new tails.
audit.microSkill: All the plus comparative with a reason
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains a cause-linked comparative without reading all as a quantity.
audit.levelReason: A less transparent degree construction supports B2 interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: A reason amplifying a comparative, not the paired the more construction.

items.setupText: An adviser says, 'No other form in this packet is as confusing as the registration form.'
items.taskText: Which ranking follows in the ordinary degree reading?
options: The registration form is more confusing than every other form in the packet.
The registration form ties with at least one other for most confusing.
At least one form is more confusing than the registration form.
The registration form is the most confusing form the adviser has ever seen.
items.answer: The registration form is more confusing than every other form in the packet.
items.explanation: No other form reaches its degree of confusion; the sentence gives it the top position without a tie in this packet.

rationales.The registration form is more confusing: No other form reaches its degree of confusion; the sentence gives it the top position without a tie in this packet.
rationales.The registration form ties with at least: A tied form would be as confusing, which no other excludes.
rationales.At least one form is more confusing than: A more confusing form would exceed the level that no other says any form reaches.
rationales.The registration form is the most confus: The comparison set is this packet, not the adviser's entire experience.

findings: The original no-other item only tested as/as connectors with malformed alternatives and stock explanation.
audit.microSkill: No other with an equality comparison yielding a unique maximum
audit.pedagogicalValue: Tracks both the absence of ties and the bounded comparison set.
audit.levelReason: A negative quantifier interacting with degree equality creates a B2 inference.
audit.similarityNote: Unique-ranking logic, not merely choosing an as ... as connector.

items.setupText: A: 'Was the checklist useful?' B: 'More than useful. It prevented us from sending the wrong files.'
items.taskText: What does B's reply do?
options: It compares the number of checklists with the number of files.
It contrasts the checklist's usefulness with its accuracy.
It limits the checklist's usefulness to correcting earlier mistakes.
It treats useful as too weak a description of the checklist's value.
items.answer: It treats useful as too weak a description of the checklist's value.
items.explanation: More than useful upgrades A's description; the prevented mistake supplies a reason for the stronger praise.

rationales.It compares the number of checklists wit: More than modifies the assessment useful, not a count of objects.
rationales.It treats useful as too weak a descripti: More than useful upgrades A's description; the prevented mistake supplies a reason for the stronger praise.
rationales.It contrasts the checklist's usefulness: No separate quality such as accuracy is introduced as the comparison point.
rationales.It limits the checklist's usefulness to: The example concerns preventing a mistake, and the phrase strengthens rather than restricts the praise.

findings: This repeated the most-useful report item with chart substituted and an irrelevant data-check tail.
audit.microSkill: More than plus adjective as an evaluative upgrade
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes comparison operating on the adequacy of a description.
audit.levelReason: A short exchange requires interpreting a nonliteral degree response.
audit.similarityNote: Upgrades a label rather than comparing two objects or numerical amounts.

items.setupText: The technician says, 'The damaged cable is less of a problem than the missing software.'
items.taskText: Which paraphrase preserves the comparison?
options: The cable is damaged to a lesser physical extent than the software.
The missing software presents the greater difficulty.
The cable has fewer individual faults than the software.
The cable is not a problem once the software is installed.
items.answer: The missing software presents the greater difficulty.
items.explanation: Less of a problem grades how serious an issue is; the cable is below the missing software on that scale.

rationales.The cable is damaged to a lesser physica: Less of a problem compares difficulty caused, not the physical extent of damage to each item.
rationales.The cable has fewer individual faults th: The sentence compares overall difficulty, not counts of faults.
rationales.The missing software presents the greate: Less of a problem grades how serious an issue is; the cable is below the missing software on that scale.
rationales.The cable is not a problem once the soft: A smaller problem is still compatible with a problem; the sentence gives no condition that removes it.

findings: The far-more-clear chart item was duplicated with a training-portal tail and trivial foils.
audit.microSkill: Less of a plus noun grading a category
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how a noun such as problem can be compared by degree through less of a.
audit.levelReason: The noun-based degree pattern extends beyond ordinary comparative adjectives.
audit.similarityNote: Degree of a problem, not a comparison of countable problems.

items.setupText: At a ticket desk, a traveller asks, 'Would it be any cheaper to return on Tuesday?'
items.taskText: What is the traveller asking about?
options: Which Tuesday service has the lowest price of all services
Whether changing the return day would reduce the price at all
Whether Tuesday's price would be lower by a particular amount
Whether a Tuesday return is cheaper than every other return day
items.answer: Whether changing the return day would reduce the price at all
items.explanation: Any before cheaper asks whether even some reduction is available, without specifying its size.

rationales.Which Tuesday service has the lowest pri: The question compares the proposed change with the current plan; it does not request a ranking of every Tuesday service.
rationales.Whether Tuesday's price would be lower b: Any cheaper leaves the amount open rather than naming a required saving.
rationales.Whether a Tuesday return is cheaper than: No comparison with every other day is stated.
rationales.Whether changing the return day would re: Any before cheaper asks whether even some reduction is available, without specifying its size.

findings: The three-schedule price item repeated 783 under a contract tail and inaccurate explanation.
audit.microSkill: Any modifying a comparative in a question
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an open inquiry about improvement from a fixed saving or global minimum.
audit.levelReason: A practical conditional question carries a subtle degree modifier.
audit.similarityNote: Open degree in an inquiry, not a declared ranking.

items.setupText: An editor observes, 'The more detail we add, the less readable the guide becomes.'
items.taskText: Which pattern does the editor describe?
options: Both detail and readability increase together.
Readability falls as the amount of detail rises.
Detail is being removed because readability has already fallen.
The guide becomes less detailed as readers gain experience.
items.answer: Readability falls as the amount of detail rises.
items.explanation: The paired comparatives move in opposite directions: more detail accompanies less readability.

rationales.Readability falls as the amount of detai: The paired comparatives move in opposite directions: more detail accompanies less readability.
rationales.Both detail and readability increase tog: Less readable marks a decrease in readability, not an increase.
rationales.Detail is being removed because readabil: The sentence describes adding detail and the associated change, not a decision to remove it.
rationales.The guide becomes less detailed as reade: Neither removal of detail nor readers' experience is the stated changing factor.

findings: The slightly-easier instructions item was another duplicate with basic form giveaways.
audit.microSkill: Opposing directions in paired comparatives
audit.pedagogicalValue: Tracks an inverse relationship between two different scales.
audit.levelReason: Two changing dimensions and opposite comparative directions suit B2 reading.
audit.similarityNote: An inverse editorial relationship, contrasting with A1-style single-scale changes.

items.setupText: A profile must give equal weight to Tessa's roles as designer and manager, without claiming how she divides her hours.
items.taskText: Which sentence achieves that writing goal?
options: Tessa spends as much time managing as designing.
Tessa is as much a manager as she is a designer.
Tessa is more a manager than a designer.
Tessa manages as many designers as the other managers do.
items.answer: Tessa is as much a manager as she is a designer.
items.explanation: As much a ... as gives the roles equal standing without measuring time spent on them.

rationales.Tessa spends as much time managing as de: This compares hours, which the writing goal explicitly leaves unclaimed.
rationales.Tessa is as much a manager as she is a d: As much a ... as gives the roles equal standing without measuring time spent on them.
More ... than gives the managerial role greater weight rather than equal weight.
rationales.Tessa manages as many designers as the o: This compares staff numbers, not the importance of her two roles.

findings: The no-other-form item repeated the same connector task under a planning-call tail.
audit.microSkill: As much a ... as comparing roles
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates equal role characterization from equal time or headcount.
audit.levelReason: A constrained profile edit requires understanding noun-phrase degree comparison.
audit.similarityNote: Equal role standing; distinct from less of a problem and ordinary as much money.

items.setupText: An organiser writes, 'More people registered than there are seats in the hall.'
items.taskText: Which relationship is asserted?
options: The hall has more seats than registered people.
The number attending exceeds the number registered.
The registration count exceeds the seating capacity.
The hall needs more seats than any other hall.
items.answer: The registration count exceeds the seating capacity.
items.explanation: The than-clause supplies the seat count as the standard for the number of people registered.

rationales.The hall has more seats than registered: That reverses which quantity is greater.
rationales.The number attending exceeds the number: The sentence compares registrations with seats, not attendance with registration.
rationales.The registration count exceeds the seati: The than-clause supplies the seat count as the standard for the number of people registered.
rationales.The hall needs more seats than any other: No other hall appears in the comparison.

findings: The most-useful lesson-plan item merely replaced a noun in the repeated folder frame.
audit.microSkill: A comparative clause comparing counts of unlike entities
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes that counts may be compared even when the counted things differ.
audit.levelReason: A full than-clause with there are requires intermediate clause comprehension.
audit.similarityNote: People-to-seat quantities, distinct from the clarity edit comparing rents rather than cities.

items.setupText: A pass cost $100 last year and costs $80 this year.
items.taskText: Which statement accurately compares the new price with last year's price?
options: This year's price is 80% lower than last year's.
Last year's price was 20% higher than this year's.
This year's price has fallen to 20% of last year's.
This year's price is 20% lower than last year's.
items.answer: This year's price is 20% lower than last year's.
items.explanation: The decrease is twenty dollars out of the old hundred-dollar price, so the reduction is 20%.

rationales.This year's price is 80% lower than last: Eighty percent lower would leave a twenty-dollar price; eighty dollars is 80% of the old price.
rationales.Last year's price was 20% higher than th: The reverse percentage uses eighty as its base; twenty dollars is 25% of eighty, not 20%.
rationales.This year's price has fallen to 20% of l: To 20% describes a twenty-dollar final price rather than the twenty-dollar decrease.
rationales.This year's price is 20% lower than last: The decrease is twenty dollars out of the old hundred-dollar price, so the reduction is 20%.

findings: The far-more-clear chart item repeated the same scrambled phrase choices without B2 demand.
audit.microSkill: Percentage comparison and its reference amount
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes lower by a percentage, lower to a proportion, and the reversed baseline.
audit.levelReason: Simple numbers support a language-focused percentage relation with a changing reference base.
audit.similarityNote: Percentage difference rather than the earlier straightforward two-to-one ratio.

items.setupText: A shop advertises, 'Selected desks: up to 30% cheaper than last month.'
items.taskText: What does this wording allow?
options: Every desk in the shop has a 30% reduction.
Thirty percent is the minimum reduction for selected desks.
Some selected desks may have a reduction smaller than 30%.
The desks now cost 30% of last month's prices.
items.answer: Some selected desks may have a reduction smaller than 30%.
items.explanation: Up to sets an upper limit on the advertised reduction; it does not give every selected desk the maximum discount.

rationales.Some selected desks may have a reduction: Up to sets an upper limit on the advertised reduction; it does not give every selected desk the maximum discount.
rationales.Every desk in the shop has a 30% reducti: Selected restricts the stock, and up to does not promise the maximum for every selected item.
rationales.Thirty percent is the minimum reduction: Up to makes 30% the upper, not the lower, limit.
rationales.The desks now cost 30% of last month's p: 'Thirty percent cheaper' means a reduction from the old price, not a final price equal to 30% of it.

findings: The least-expensive schedules were reused a third time with a board-discussion tail.
audit.microSkill: Up to limiting a comparative discount
audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets an advertised maximum without converting it into a universal or minimum reduction.
audit.levelReason: A compact commercial comparison combines degree limits with restricted stock.
audit.similarityNote: Maximum possible reduction across products, not a fixed percentage calculation.

items.setupText: A report says the new system processed nearly twice as many requests as the old one under the same test conditions.
items.taskText: Which count pair best fits that description?
options: Old: 100 requests; new: 105 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 195 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 205 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 295 requests
items.answer: Old: 100 requests; new: 195 requests
items.explanation: Nearly twice as many places the new count close to, but below, two times the old count.

rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 105 requests: That is only slightly more, not close to double.
rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 195 requests: Nearly twice as many places the new count close to, but below, two times the old count.
rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 205 requests: This is slightly more than twice as many, not nearly twice in the ordinary below-target reading.
rationales.Old: 100 requests; new: 295 requests: That is nearly three times the old count, not nearly twice.

findings: The slightly-easier item again repeated elementary adverb selection under a procedure tail.
audit.microSkill: Nearly modifying a multiplier comparison
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps closeness to a multiple distinct from a small increase or an overshoot.
audit.levelReason: Round counts make the interaction of nearly and twice the central challenge.
audit.similarityNote: Approximate ratio with a directional modifier, beyond exact twice as many.

items.setupText: After a supposed consultation, a resident says, 'It felt more like a sales presentation than a discussion.'
items.taskText: What is being compared?
options: The number of sales presentations and discussions held
The resident's preference for presentations over discussions
The meeting's resemblance to two kinds of event
The duration of the sales and discussion portions
items.answer: The meeting's resemblance to two kinds of event
items.explanation: More like ... than compares how well two descriptions fit the same experience.

rationales.The number of sales presentations and di: More modifies like here, not a count of events.
rationales.The resident's preference for presentati: The sentence characterizes what the meeting resembled; it does not say which event the resident prefers.
rationales.The meeting's resemblance to two kinds o: More like ... than compares how well two descriptions fit the same experience.
rationales.The duration of the sales and discussion: The comparison concerns resemblance, not explicitly the time spent on separate portions.

findings: The no-other-form connector item was repeated with only a service-report tail.
audit.microSkill: More like ... than comparing resemblance
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes comparison between possible descriptions of one event.
audit.levelReason: An evaluative comment requires separating resemblance from preference and quantity.
audit.similarityNote: Resemblance frame, avoiding the Gerunds topic's not so much ... as frame.

items.setupText: A report calls a design 'the best of the three we tested.' An editor changes this to 'the best possible design.'
items.taskText: How does the edit change the comparison?
options: It expands the ranking claim beyond the three tested designs.
It limits the claim to designs that passed the test.
It changes the design from best to merely acceptable.
It makes the claim depend only on the most recent test.

items.answer: A ratio of delay probabilities does not give the same inverse ratio for their complements.
